title: End-to-end latency budgets
summary: A latency budget splits a target such as time to first token into stage allowances. Run independent stages in parallel, watch the tail not the mean, and attack the stage that dominates before touching the others.
useIf: A request crosses several stages (auth, rewrite, retrieval, guards, model, output checks) and you must hit a latency target.
avoidIf: The system is a single model call with no other stages. Use the TTFT and TPOT topics directly.

explain.md: Pick the number the user feels, usually TTFT for a streamed chat or TTLT for a programmatic call, then give each stage an allowance and measure p50 and p95 per stage. Total latency is the sum along the **critical path**, not the sum of all stages. Stages that do not depend on each other, such as an input guard and retrieval, can run in parallel and drop off the path [[r14]] [[r15]].

explain.md: Run sequentially, these sum to 1,340 ms. With the guard in parallel the path is 1,260 ms. Dropping the LLM rewrite for standalone queries gives 1,010 ms. Each step is a different dial, and the lab below lets you try them together.

explain.intro: Load the Interactive chat preset and find where first-token time goes. Turn on the parallel guard, then streaming, then a prompt cache hit (it cuts model TTFT by an assumed 50%), then the smaller-model toggle. Finally set every p95 to 3 times its p50 and compare the typical path, the simulated p95 and the sum of the p95s. All defaults are illustrative, not product measurements.

explain.md: **Tails.** The sum of stage p95s overstates the end-to-end p95, but fan-out makes the slowest call decide. If each of 100 parallel calls is slow 1% of the time, 63% of requests see at least one slow call [[tr4]]. Defences are per-stage deadlines, a fallback when a stage is late (skip the rerank, serve without the rewrite) and **hedged requests**: after about the p95 delay send a duplicate and take the first reply. In a Google benchmark a 10 ms hedge cut the 99.9th percentile of 1,000 reads from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for 2% more requests [[tr4]].

**Streaming and guards.** Streaming lowers perceived latency but not total time [[r14]]. An output guard that needs the whole answer defeats it, so budget TTLT, or guard in chunks. Pair latency with output token counts, and set separate SLIs: TTFT p95, TTLT p95 per output-length bucket, and cache hit ratio [[r14]].

whereToUse: RAG assistants with rewrite, retrieval, rerank, guard and generation stages
Agents that fan out to many tool calls and wait for the slowest
Voice and live-assist products with a hard first-response budget
Gateway designs that add token limits, content safety and caching in front of the model
Incident reviews that ask which stage moved the p95

use: More than one stage contributes noticeable time before the first token
Some stages are independent and could run in parallel
You have per-stage percentiles from traces, not only an end-to-end average
avoid: Treating the sum of p95s as the p95 of the whole path
Optimising a stage that is under 5% of the path while the model call is 60%
Budgeting only for p50 when the product promise is a tail percentile
flips: An output guard needs the full text: the target becomes TTLT, so stream status and guard in chunks if allowed
Fan-out grows: tail amplification matters more than any single stage's p50
The model call dominates: use caching, a smaller or routed model and shorter output before tuning the rest

pitfalls.symptom: Mean latency improved but complaints continue
pitfalls.cause: The tail moved little, or fan-out makes slow calls common
pitfalls.fix: Track p95 and p99 per stage, add deadlines and hedge idempotent reads [[tr4]]

pitfalls.symptom: Streaming was enabled and the first word is still late
pitfalls.cause: TTFT is dominated by stages before the model, such as rewrite and rerank
pitfalls.fix: Chart the budget by stage and shorten or parallelise the biggest pre-model stage

pitfalls.symptom: A regression is blamed on infrastructure
pitfalls.cause: Answers got longer, which raises TTLT but not TTFT
pitfalls.fix: Bucket TTLT by output tokens before opening an incident [[r14]]

scenarios.title: Chat that must start in 1.2 seconds
scenarios.situation: An interactive RAG assistant takes 1,340 ms to the first token at p50 on the illustrative budget above. The product target is 1,200 ms at p50 and 1,800 ms at p95. Answers stream.
constraints: Stages: auth, rewrite, embed, retrieve, rerank, guard, assembly, model, network
Quality must not drop for hard queries
unknowns: What share of queries need the LLM rewrite?
Is a stable prefix available for caching?
scenarios.question: Which changes do you make first?

options.name: Run the input guard beside retrieval and skip the rewrite for standalone queries, then cache the stable prefix
options.why: The guard drops 80 ms and the skipped rewrite 250 ms for most queries, taking the path to about 1,010 ms. A prefix cache then trims model TTFT.
options.tradeoff: Hard follow-up queries still need the rewrite, so route by a cheap check.

options.name: Turn on streaming
options.why: It is already on. Streaming changes perceived total time, not the time before the first token.
options.tradeoff: Right when the target is felt completion time and answers are long.

options.name: Switch to a smaller model
options.tradeoff: It risks quality, and the larger savings are available without that risk.

flips.if: Guard policy forbids running before retrieval completes
flips.then: Keep it sequential and focus on the rewrite and prefix cache.

flips.if: Model TTFT is 60% of the path after changes
flips.then: Move to caching and model choice next.

scenarios.takeaway: Remove or overlap pre-model stages before spending quality on the model.

scenarios.title: Agent step that waits on 20 tool calls
scenarios.situation: An agent step issues 20 read-only calls in parallel and waits for all. Each call has a p50 of 120 ms and 1% of calls take over 2 seconds. Users see the step stall about one in five times.
constraints: A partial answer is acceptable for non-critical sources
scenarios.question: How do you protect the tail?

options.name: Set per-call deadlines, hedge idempotent reads after about the p95 delay, and degrade when non-critical sources are late
options.why: With 20 calls the chance of one slow call is about 18%, so tail control matters. Hedging is cheap for idempotent reads and a deadline bounds the step.
options.tradeoff: Hedges add a small share of extra calls and need cancellation of the loser.

options.name: Retry every timeout immediately and without limit
options.why: It multiplies load during incidents and still waits for the slowest retry.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a single rare call, with backoff and a cap.

options.name: Raise the timeout so slow calls finish
options.tradeoff: The step waits for the slowest call, so the stall remains.

flips.if: Calls are not idempotent or are costly
flips.then: Do not hedge. Use deadlines and fallbacks only.
The tail matters far less. Simple deadlines may be enough.

scenarios.takeaway: Fan-out turns rare slow calls into common slow requests.

quiz.q: Stages in ms: auth 20, rewrite 250, embed 60, retrieve 120, rerank 150, input guard 80, assembly 10, model TTFT 600, network 50. The guard runs in parallel with embed, retrieve and rerank. What is the time to first token in ms?
quiz.hint: The parallel branch costs the longer of 80 and 60 + 120 + 150
quiz.explain: 20 + 250 + max(80, 330) + 10 + 600 + 50 = 1,260. Without the overlap the sum is 1,340, so the guard hides 80 ms.

quiz.q: A request fans out to 100 parallel calls and each call is slow 1% of the time, independently. What percentage of requests see at least one slow call?
quiz.explain: 0.99^100 is about 0.366, so 1 - 0.366 = 0.634. The Tail at Scale paper states the 63% figure for this case.

quiz.q: When are hedged requests an appropriate defence against tail latency?
options: For non-idempotent writes that must run once
For cheap, idempotent calls, sent after about the p95 delay with the loser cancelled
For every call from the first attempt, to be safe
Only when the mean is already low
quiz.explain: Hedging duplicates work, so it fits idempotent, cheap calls and is triggered late to cap extra load. Duplicating writes is unsafe, hedging everything doubles cost, and the mean is not the trigger.

flashcards.front: What is the critical path in a latency budget?
flashcards.back: The longest chain of dependent stages. Stages that overlap, such as a guard beside retrieval, add only if they are longer than the chain they overlap.

flashcards.front: Why does fan-out make the tail matter?
flashcards.back: With 100 parallel calls that are each slow 1% of the time, 63% of requests see at least one slow call.

flashcards.front: What did the Tail at Scale benchmark show for hedging?
flashcards.back: A 10 ms hedge cut the 99.9th percentile of 1,000 reads from 1,800 ms to 74 ms for about 2% more requests.
